claims.label: supported
claims.claim_summary: Qwen3.6-27B with MASS achieves 1.2-1.6x higher token efficiency on public benchmarks.
claims.claim_text_verbatim: Over two MASS cycles with Qwen3.6-27B, the model achieves 1.2–1.6× higher performance per output tokens on four open-ended public benchmarks.

evidence_spans.source_text: Arrows go from L(0) to L(2), labelled with the ratio of their score per output token: on the four research benchmarks (top row, bottom left), L(2) gains 1.2–1.6×.
Figure 2 further compares score per output token: on these four research benchmarks, L(2) achieves 1.2–1.6× higher score per output token than L(0).

claims.label: partially_supported
claims.claim_summary: MASS enables continuous recursive bootstrapping as the model becomes a better optimizer and evaluator.
claims.claim_text_verbatim: Because the improved model subsequently acts as a better optimizer and evaluator, this alternating framework enables a continuous, recursive bootstrapping of the model’s capabilities.

evidence_spans.source_text: The agreement increases from 0.73 for L(0) to 0.91 for L(1) and 0.93 for L(2).
In this transfer setting, workflows optimized by L(1) outperform those optimized by L(0) in 64% of comparisons on average across 11 iterations and 12 tasks.
The recursive loop here is empirical. Unlike proof-based self-rewriting in Gödel machines (Schmidhuber, 2007), it provides no guarantee that every future cycle improves.
In percentages, the results are 37.5 ± 2.2, 35.3 ± 2.1, and 35.2 ± 1.7 for L(0), L(1), and L(2), respectively.

claims.label: partially_supported
claims.claim_summary: Multi-agent traces outperform single-agent training despite using 1.4x fewer tokens.
claims.claim_text_verbatim: Moreover, multi-agent traces are also more training-efficient: a student trained on them outperforms a single-agent student trained on 1.4× more training tokens.

evidence_spans.source_text: More directly, M + reaches 68.3% with 28.82M processed supervised tokens, 4.3 points above S++ while using 31.4% fewer tokens.
Likewise, the M + versus S++ comparison uses their scores against the base, not a direct head-to-head comparison.
M + has broader training-task coverage and a different sampler, so it is not a matched-data control.
These differences in sampling, data, and checkpoint selection limit what can be attributed to teacher composition alone.

claims.label: partially_supported
claims.claim_summary: Optimization increases task-specific routing information while reducing cross-component redundancy.
claims.claim_text_verbatim: Optimized workflows increasingly place task-specific information in what agents communicate and how they are routed, while reducing redundant information across workflow components.

evidence_spans.source_text: In all four encoder/estimator configurations, roles and instructions decrease while contracts and hops increase between i = 3 and i = 11 (arrows).

Unconditional total correlation falls in all four encoder/estimator combinations. The task-centered estimate falls in three; permutation-adjusted MPNet is the exception. Intermediate values need not be monotone.
The estimates are descriptive text statistics, rather than measurements of messages exchanged during execution or a causal test of the proposed learning mechanism.

claims.label: supported
claims.claim_summary: Delegation and code handoff occurrences increase dramatically across generations without prompting.
claims.claim_text_verbatim: Delegation rises from 1/110 trajectories for L(0) to 48/110 for L(1) and 87/110 for L(2), while code handoffs rise from 1/110 to 42/110 and 83/110, respectively.

evidence_spans.source_text: Delegation (D) means that the orchestrator calls a subagent and the call returns without a tool error.
A code handoff (H) occurs when a subagent successfully reads a Python file whose latest recorded writer is a different subagent that has already returned.
